title: The Majestic One?: Prelude and Fugue No.8, Book I
content_blocks: This piece was the second of all of the preludes and fugues that I wrote, but the last one using the “arithmetic scale” that had been a feature of my music for more than a decade.  This scale starts with one half-step, then two, then three, etc.  It’s the same forward and backward, the same upside down and right side up, but most interestingly it moves from one familiar major or minor key area immediately into another that is a tritone away—creating a fascinating mix of familiarity and surprise.

The prelude is built around four-note chords built from segments of the mode.  These chords range in total span from a perfect fourth (at the narrowest) to two-and-one-half octaves (at the widest).  Each successively larger (or smaller) four-note-chord is transposed so that it contains the G above middle C.

Most of the resulting sonorities struck me as the type of harmonies that Messiaen would use, so I decided to emulate him. I arranged these chords as a repeating series of chords and a repeating series of rhythms that don’t line up (following Messaien’s take on isorhythm)— except that there are two different repeating series of chords and two different repeating series of rhythms. The overall effect is one of a Messiaen-like series of chords with a sense of an underlying logic that is, somehow, imperceptible, and which projects a sense of G as “tonic.” On top of this harmonic series snatches of a melody are played, part of which is reminiscent of Messiaen’s Quartet for the End of Time.

The Fugue takes a cue from the Prelude, combining two different simultaneous melodic presentations of the scale. Gesturally, the subject of the fugue recalls the subject of the D major fugue from the first book of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier: a sudden burst of notes as the start (“head”) of the subject, followed by a constrained melodic line. The head is, at times, detached from the rest of the subject and overlapped with itself, creating a series of as many as 24 rapid notes one after another.

Steve Beck brings out the intended timelessness of the Prelude, and the turning-on-a-dime shifts in the Fugue. As you can see in this combined video, he also brings an intensity, focus, and musical appreciation that I love—check out his expressions throughout, but especially at about 6:56 into the video. As for the title of this blogpost, well, the tempo marking for the Fugue is Maestoso, con fuoco (majestic, with fire), so I called the pair “The Majestic One” back in 2021. Does it apply to the Prelude? Is it a good fit for the pair? Listening to Steve’s performance makes me think that it is a good fit, but please let me know!
